Module 3 · Lesson 3

Deliberate Practice & Specificity of Practice

Getting better is not just a matter of repeating a skill. The kind of practice you do — and the conditions you practice in — shape what you ultimately learn.

~30 min Builds on Lessons 1–2 Prepares simulation & VR
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to…

  • 1Distinguish naïve, purposeful, and deliberate practice.
  • 2Describe the role of deliberate practice in developing expertise and explain Ericsson’s expertise approach.
  • 3Explain why the popular “10,000-hour rule” oversimplifies the research on expert performance.
  • 4Explain the specificity of practice principle and how practice conditions influence later performance.
Before we start

Think of a skill you know how to do

Choose one motor skill you have learned — a sport skill, instrument, clinical task, dance, driving, or anything else.

Your starting point

What kind of practice did you do? How much did you practice? Would you call yourself an expert, or simply “good” at the skill?

Most importantly: what separates an expert from someone who can perform the skill reasonably well?

This is a personal thinking prompt — it is not submitted or graded. Your text is saved on this device only.

We’ll return to your example after defining three very different kinds of practice.

Types of practice

Not all practice is the same

Select each practice type to reveal what distinguishes it.

Naïve practice+

Activities done for enjoyment or general engagement.

  • Casual play
  • Unstructured repetition
  • Can support initial learning
  • Not sufficient for expertise
Purposeful practice+

Individualized activities the learner uses specifically to improve performance.

  • Clear intent to improve
  • Often organized or self-directed
  • No expert teacher providing immediate individualized guidance
Deliberate practice+

Highly structured activity designed specifically to improve performance.

  • Clear goals
  • Immediate feedback
  • Error correction and refinement
  • Effort and full attention
  • Pushes beyond the comfort zone
The key distinction

More practice time does not automatically mean better practice. The structure, feedback, goals, and attention devoted to the task matter.

One skill, three approaches

Learning guitar as an example

Naïve

Strumming and changing chords for a few minutes whenever a guitar happens to be available.

Purposeful

Following a book or online resource to learn specific guitar skills, without a live teacher providing immediate personalized feedback.

Deliberate

A teacher identifies weak areas, gives immediate feedback, sets specific goals, and pushes the learner beyond comfortable performance.

Knowledge check

What kind of practice is this?

Classify each example. Answer all three to continue.

1. A student casually shoots baskets with friends, mostly for fun, without tracking errors or setting a goal.

2. A learner follows a structured online piano program, practices weak passages, and tracks progress — but works without a knowledgeable teacher providing immediate individualized feedback.

3. A coach watches a swimmer, identifies a technical weakness, assigns a demanding drill, and gives immediate feedback after each attempt.

Answer all three to continue.

Study of human expertise

Reverse-engineering expert performance

K. Anders Ericsson studied expert performance in areas such as medicine, music, chess, and sports, with a strong focus on extended deliberate practice.

His expertise approach starts with elite performers and asks how they got there — essentially “reverse engineering” expertise.

The research question changes

Instead of asking only which practice condition improves performance in a short experiment, the expertise approach asks what years of practice look like in people who eventually reach very high levels of performance.

A framework for skill development

Fitts & Posner: three stages of learning

Fitts and Posner described motor-skill learning as a progression through three broad stages. The important idea is that the learner’s needs change as the skill becomes more established.

1

Cognitive stage

The learner is figuring out what to do. Performance requires substantial attention and conscious thought.

2

Associative stage

The basic pattern is established. Practice is increasingly about refining the movement, reducing errors, and becoming more consistent.

3

Autonomous stage

The skill can be performed with much less conscious attention. Execution becomes more automatic.

Why this matters for deliberate practice

Becoming automatic is useful — but automatic performance is not the same thing as expert performance. Once a skill feels easy, continued improvement requires practice that deliberately identifies weaknesses and creates new challenges.

Development of expert performance

Automatic is useful — but it can also become a ceiling

Now apply the Fitts and Posner framework to a question about expertise: what happens after a skill reaches the autonomous stage and can be performed with little conscious effort?

Ericsson’s argument

If a learner simply repeats an already-automatic skill without deliberate practice, performance may stop developing. Deliberate practice keeps exposing weaknesses, correcting errors, and adapting the skill to new challenges.

How expertise is studied

Estimating a lifetime of practice

One method used in expertise research is the retrospective estimation technique: asking performers to estimate how much time they devoted to practicing a skill across different periods of their lives.

Accumulated practice

Where the “10,000 hours” number came from

Ericsson and colleagues (1993) documented estimated accumulated practice among young violinists from about age 5 to 20.

Important word: average

The 10,000-hour value was an average for one group in one domain — not a universal biological threshold for expertise.

Knowledge check

What did the research actually say?

Judge each statement. Answer all three to continue.

1. Exactly 10,000 hours of practice is a universal requirement for becoming world-class in any skill.

2. The 10,000-hour figure was an average amount of deliberate practice accumulated by the best violinists by about age 20.

3. The type and quality of practice matter; simply accumulating 10,000 hours of any kind of repetition is not the point.

Answer all three to continue.

Was your approach to practice mostly naïve, purposeful, or deliberate? What specific features of your practice make you classify it that way?

Core principle

Specificity of Practice

What you learn depends largely on what you practice — including the conditions in which you practice it.

Practicing in a particular environment or workspace often produces the best performance in that same environment or workspace. The sensory feedback that accompanies performance becomes part of the learned skill.

Simple version

If you want to get better at a particular task, practice should resemble the actual performance as closely as possible.

What becomes part of the skill?

Practice conditions are information

Specificity is not only about the movement itself. The information and context surrounding the movement can become part of what is learned.

V

Visual

What you see while performing.

A

Auditory

Sounds and noise in the environment.

T

Tactile

Feel of surfaces, tools, and contact.

C

Context

Workspace, pressure, and performance conditions.

Example

Studying for a high-stakes exam in a comfortable setting is not identical to performing under the pressure of the real exam. Practice under more similar conditions can better prepare you for those demands.

Practice specificity in the real world

Same principle, very different settings

Surgical training

A high-fidelity laparoscopic simulator shares more of the target task’s demands than a generic dexterity exercise, so it should support better transfer to the operating room.

Rehabilitation

A patient who practices walking only in a therapy gym may still struggle on uneven outdoor surfaces because those conditions were not part of practice.

Knowledge check

Which practice plan is more specific?

Choose the practice option that more closely matches the target performance.

1. A patient ultimately needs to walk safely on uneven sidewalks.

2. A basketball player must make free throws in a noisy game.

3. A learner needs to perform a clinical task using the actual tools and workspace.

Answer all three to continue.

Connecting back to transfer

Transfer happens — but specificity is usually stronger

Practicing suturing on a grape or banana can provide a useful starting point. Some elements of the skill can transfer.

But if the goal is to suture a real wound, fruit practice alone cannot reproduce all of the task’s tactile, visual, and contextual demands.

The practical implication

Early practice can use simplified or safer versions of a task, but proficiency in the target task requires practice that becomes increasingly similar to the real performance conditions.

Wrap up

What you can now do

  • 1Tell naïve, purposeful, and deliberate practice apart based on goals, structure, feedback, and effort.
  • 2Explain why extended deliberate practice is central to Ericsson’s account of expert performance and why routine repetition can lead to arrested development.
  • 3Explain why the 10,000-hour rule is an oversimplification rather than a universal threshold.
  • 4Apply specificity of practice: later performance is strongest when practice reproduces the movements, information, and conditions required by the target task.
Next: simulation and virtual reality

Specificity creates an immediate practical question: what if the real task is too dangerous, expensive, unavailable, or impractical to practice directly? Simulation and VR try to recreate the important elements of the real task — and their value depends on how well that training transfers.
